newsitem.title: THAILAND: Relief in Thailand over fair Yankee bond pricing.
newsitem.headline: Relief in Thailand over fair Yankee bond pricing.

text.p: Thai officials and analysts expressed relief on Friday that Thailand's $600 million Yankee bond issue won moderate U.S. pricing despite Moody's downgrade of the country's ratings,
This reflected market confidence in Thailand despite its economic problems, they said. They also noted the issue was initially for $500 million but was increased by $100 million.

Thailand's economic growth has slowed sharply since 1996 and its financial system has been shaken by billions of dollars in sour loans extended to a troubled property sector. Export growth has also slowed.

The 10-year bond pricing, at 90 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, took into account Moody's Investors Service lowering this week of Thailand's foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits to A3 from A2, analysts told Reuters.

"This is positive news. The pricing is fair and the Moody's downgrade helped clear earlier market doubt about Thailand's credit standing," said Somchai Trairatpirom, head of research at SITCA Investment and Securities Plc.

A Finance Ministry official said the pricing reflected Thailand's new credit ratings and a relatively volatile U.S. bond market outlook amid current expectations that the Federal Reserve Board could raise interest rates soon.

"The pricing and spread that we got is acceptable even though the issue's timing may not be ideal. We have been prepared for a negative impact of the Moody's downgrade," said the official, who declined to be identified.

"The issue was also priced at a time the Fed was expected to raise its rates," she added. Without the Moody's downgrade, the Thai issue would have been priced at 65-70 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Brett Williams of Krungthai Thanakit Plc described the issue as Thailand's first successful foray into the Yankee bond market in five years.

"It was very cheap and conservatively priced against the backdrop of a very skittish outlook of the U.S. debt market and the fact that savvy U.S. investors are well aware of current Thai economic problems," he said.
Among other South East Asian sovereigns, Indonesia's 10-year bond -- rated three notches lower at Baa3 by Moody's -- was trading at 100 basis points over Treasuries.

Somchai of SITCA said both the Thai and Indonesian pricing fairly reflected their respective Moody's ratings. "The Thai pricing looks strictly in line with Moody's new rating on the country without involving any premium or discount."
The Finance Ministry official said Moody's lower ratings for Thailand were partly offset by S&P's recent decision to maintain its current single A rating for the country.
She said Thailand decided to scrap a plan to split the Yankee issue into 10- and 30-year tranches, partly at the request of state enterprises which would utilise funds raised.
"They think 30 years was too long and that could entail higher financing cost," she said.
